title: The Tell: Bets on falling volatility now ‘most crowded trade’: fund managers
text:
Published: Jan 16, 2018 10:05 a.m. ET Share 
Investors expect bull market in stocks to run until 2019 Getty Images William Watts Deputy markets editor 
Global investors are betting on a continued rise in equities, are unhedged, and look for the bull market in stocks to continue until 2019, according to the latest monthly survey of global fund managers conducted by Bank of America Merrill Lynch. 
That said, fund managers for the first time worried that bets on falling volatility are now the “most crowded” trade, overtaking bets on bitcoin and FAANG+BAT—an acronym combo referring to U.S. tech giants Facebook Inc. FB, +0.77% , Apple Inc. AAPL, +1.23% , Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, +1.98% , Netflix Inc. NFLX, +1.23% and Google parent Alphabet Inc. GOOG, +1.10% and Chinese tech giants Baidu BIDU, +4.75% , Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. BABA, +1.58% and Tencent Holdings Ltd. 0700, +2.54% . 
Volatility has remained quite subdued, with the CBOE Volatility Index, or VIX VIX, +7.78% trading near all-time lows over much of 2017. The survey marked the first time worries about short volatility trades have topped the list. This should be worrying--but we just don't know when. For the moment, Party on, Garth. https://t.co/dYoOtBtSsQ — Guy LeBas (@lebas_janney) January 16, 2018 
The survey, conducted between Jan. 5 and 11 and released Tuesday, found investors, who in December had forecast a second-quarter 2018 equity peak, now look for stocks to continue to rally into 2019. It also found the level of investor hedging was the lowest since January 2014. 
Stocks have started 2018 with a bang, with the S&P 500 SPX, +0.67% and other major indexes notching a string of records. 
A drop in the cash levels to 4.4% from 4.7%, marking a five-year low, wasn’t enough to trigger an equity sell signal via the bank’s Bull & Bear Indicator, said analysts at Bank of America Merrill Lynch. 
In other highlights, the survey found investors were the most overweight stocks relative to government bonds since August 2014, while the top worry for investors was of an inflation-sparked crash in the bond market that would send yields rising. The survey found inflation expectation were the fourth highest since 1995 but that asset allocators are determined to stay long unil rising rates affect earnings forecasts, BAML said. 
January asset allocation plans are pro-cyclical, with investors headed into tech, industrials, emerging markets and equities, while moving out of telecom (with the second lowest allocation since 2005), bonds, utilities, and U.K. stocks, the survey found. Related Topics
